fixes.explanation: That's the line, friend. David writes what many are saying about him: “God will not deliver him.” (Psalm 3:2). It's a heavy thing to hear about yourself. Notice that David tells it to God and doesn't keep it to himself.
A new king? Nobody in this psalm is measuring anyone for a crown. What many say is “God will not deliver him.” (Psalm 3:2). That's the whole message, and it's about whether God will rescue him.

True. David says the LORD is “…my glory, and the One who lifts my head.” (Psalm 3:3). Just before that, the psalm reports what many say about him. I think a lifted head is a mighty fine thing to have in a rough week.

David doesn't ask to be hidden. His words are, “Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!” (Psalm 3:7). He asks to be saved. I spent years hidden in the back of a junk drawer, friend, and let me tell you, hidden and saved are NOT the same thing.
I'd love to hand you forgiveness here, friend, but it's not in this verse. David says, “Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!” (Psalm 3:7). His request here is to be saved. Good answer, wrong verse.

The LORD, friend. David says, “Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people.” (Psalm 3:8). After all that talk of enemies, he lands on who saves, and then he prays for God's people. It's a great last line.
David is a king (2 Samuel 5:3), but that's not who he names. He says, “Salvation belongs to the LORD…” (Psalm 3:8). He points past himself, which I think is a humble way to end.
